iron.e: From Middle English iren, from Old English īsern, īsærn, īren, īsen, from Proto-West Germanic *īsarn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarną (“iron”), from Proto-Celtic *īsarnom (“iron”), possibly a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”).
iron.g: A common, inexpensive metal, silvery grey when untarnished, that rusts, is attracted by magnets, and is used in making steel: a chemical ele

irrational.e: From Latin irratiōnālis, from ir- + ratiōnālis.
irrational.g: Not rational; unfounded, nonsensical or wrong-headed.

irreverence.e: From Middle English irreverence, from Latin irreverentia, from irreverēns (“irreverent”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, ir- + reverence.
irreverence.g: The state or quality of being irreverent; want of proper reverence; disregard of the authority and character of a superior.

irreverent.e: From Latin irreverēns. By surface analysis, ir- + reverent.
irreverent.g: Lacking respect; not having or not showing respect for or seriousness towards something that is usually treated with respect; going against

irrevocable.e: From Middle French irrévocable, from Latin irrevocabilis; equivalent to ir- + revoke + -able.
irrevocable.g: Unable to be retracted or reversed; final.
